notes.meaning: David's oldest son, Amnon, became obsessed with Tamar, the sister of his half-brother Absalom. Both Absalom and Tamar shared the same mother, while Amnon had a different mother. Amnon claimed to love her, but his desire was really a selfish and forbidden craving.
Amnon made himself physically sick with frustration over his desire. Unmarried royal daughters lived in private quarters away from men, so Amnon had no easy way to get near her.
Amnon had a cousin named Jonadab, who was the son of David's brother. Jonadab was very clever and shrewd, but he used his mind to plan wicked schemes.

Jonadab noticed that the king's heir looked more worn out every morning, so he asked what was wrong. Amnon admitted his craving for Tamar, calling her Absalom's sister rather than his own to ease his guilt.
Jonadab gave Amnon a cunning plan. He told him to lie in bed, pretend to be sick, and ask King David to send Tamar to cook for him so he could eat from her hand.
Amnon followed the advice and played the part of a sick man. When David came to visit, Amnon asked for his sister Tamar to come and bake special cakes where he could see her.
David sent a message to Tamar's living quarters, telling her to go to Amnon's house and make food for him. Without knowing it, the king helped set the trap that placed his daughter in danger.
Tamar obeyed her father and went to Amnon's house while he lay in bed. She mixed the dough, shaped the cakes in front of him, and baked them without suspecting any harm.
Tamar served the freshly baked food, but Amnon refused to eat. Pretending that company bothered him, he ordered every servant out of the room so they would be completely alone.
Amnon told Tamar to bring the cakes into his private bedroom so he could eat directly from her hand. Trusting her brother, she walked into the inner room with the food.
When Tamar stepped close to feed him, Amnon grabbed her by force. He dropped all pretense of being an invalid and demanded that she sleep with him.
Tamar begged him to stop and refused to give in. She reminded him that such a shameful crime was strictly forbidden among God's people in Israel.
Tamar pleaded that her honor would be ruined and that Amnon would be despised as a shameless fool. She even suggested speaking to the king, trying anything she could think of to delay him and escape.
Amnon would not listen to any of her words or pleas. Because he was physically stronger, he overpowered her and raped her.
As soon as Amnon satisfied his craving, his feelings flipped into intense disgust. He hated Tamar even more than he had desired her, and he coldly ordered her to get up and leave.
Tamar told him that throwing her out was an even worse cruelty than his first crime. Casting her out into the street would ruin her future and expose her to public shame as if she were guilty.
Amnon refused to hear her and called his servant. He treated his own sister like an unwanted intruder, commanding the servant to throw her out and bolt the door behind her.
The servant forced Tamar out and locked the door. She was wearing a special colorful robe that marked her royal status as an unmarried princess, making her humiliation obvious to everyone.
Tamar put ashes on her head, tore her royal robe, and placed her hands on her head in deep grief. She walked away weeping aloud, showing the public that a terrible wrong had been done to her.

Her brother Absalom realized what happened and told her to stay quiet for the moment so he could plan his revenge. Tamar went to live in Absalom's house as a lonely, broken woman whose future was taken from her.
When King David heard about the assault, he was furious. Even so, he took no legal action to punish Amnon, partly out of fond indulgence for his oldest son and guilt over his own past sins.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Ancient Greek and Latin manuscripts add that David would not punish Amnon because he loved him as his firstborn son, an explanation included in some traditional translations.

notes.meaning: Absalom said nothing to Amnon, neither friendly words nor threats. He hid his deep hatred and pretended everything was normal while waiting for the right moment to take vengeance.

Absalom waited patiently for two full years until the seasonal sheep-shearing festival at Baal-hazor. Sheep-shearing was always a time of generous hospitality and feasting, giving him the perfect cover to invite all the king's sons.
Absalom approached David and invited the king along with his court to the celebration. He knew the king would likely decline, but the polite invitation helped hide his deadly plan.
David declined because bringing his whole royal entourage would be too costly and burdensome for his son. Though Absalom urged him, the king stood firm, gave Absalom his blessing, and stayed behind.
Absalom then asked if his older brother Amnon could attend as the king's representative. David hesitated and questioned why Amnon specifically needed to go, showing a faint flicker of concern.
Absalom kept urging his father until David finally let Amnon and the rest of the royal sons go with him. David's guard was let down, opening the door for disaster.

Absalom instructed his servants to wait until Amnon was cheerful and relaxed with wine. He told them to strike Amnon down without fear, taking full personal responsibility for the murder as their master.
Absalom's servants killed Amnon just as they were ordered. Fearing a general massacre, the other royal sons jumped onto their mules and raced away toward home.
Before the princes reached the city, an exaggerated rumor reached David claiming that Absalom had murdered all of the king's sons. Terrible news often grows larger as it travels in moments of panic.
Believing all his sons were dead, David tore his clothes and collapsed on the ground in total despair. His royal attendants tore their garments as well and stood around him in deep sorrow.
Jonadab quickly spoke up to correct the rumor and assured David that only Amnon was dead. He explained that Absalom had plotted this revenge ever since the day Amnon assaulted Tamar.
Jonadab urged the king not to grieve over the false report about all his sons. He repeated with full confidence that only Amnon was dead.

While Absalom fled into exile, a watchman on the city walls looked out and saw a large group of travelers coming down the hillside road. Absalom knew that murder carried the death penalty, so he escaped while everyone was in shock.
Jonadab told the king that the returning group was indeed the royal sons, just as he had predicted. He took credit for his insight, even though his own wicked advice had started the entire tragedy.
As Jonadab finished speaking, the king's sons walked in weeping aloud. The king and all his servants joined in, crying bitterly over the murder of the heir and the wreckage of their family.
Absalom fled to the small kingdom of Geshur to seek shelter with his grandfather, King Talmai. Meanwhile, David mourned every day over the loss of his son Amnon.
Absalom lived in safe exile in Geshur for three years. Because his mother's family ruled that land, he remained protected from Israel's laws against murder.

Over time, David's grief for Amnon subsided, and his heart began to long for Absalom's return. David loved his sons deeply, but his reluctance to enforce justice once again laid the groundwork for future heartbreak.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars translate this difficult phrase to mean that David gave up all thoughts of pursuing or punishing Absalom, rather than that he personally longed to see him.
